facts.title: Frustrating the conquistadors
facts.text: When 16th-century Spanish colonists panned for gold in the rivers of the Choco region of Colombia, they kept finding a stubborn white metal mixed in with their nuggets. They dismissively named it 'platina', meaning 'little silver', and some even threw it back into the water believing it was an unripe form of gold. It would be centuries before this 'nuisance' metal was recognized as one of the most valuable elements on Earth.

facts.title: Heavier than it looks
facts.text: Platinum is extraordinarily dense, packing about 21.45 grams into every cubic centimeter. A cube of platinum just 30 centimeters on a side would weigh roughly 580 kilograms, more than a grand piano. This density is why a small platinum ring feels noticeably heavier in the hand than a gold one of the same size.

facts.title: The metal that refuses to rust
facts.text: Platinum is one of the least reactive metals known, resisting attack from oxygen, water, and most acids even when heated. It will not dissolve in either nitric or hydrochloric acid alone, but only in a freshly mixed 3-to-1 blend of the two called aqua regia ('royal water'). This near-total corrosion resistance is why platinum survives buried in riverbeds for millions of years looking as bright as the day it formed.

facts.title: The clean-air catalyst
facts.text: The single largest use of platinum is inside the catalytic converters of cars, where a thin coating of the metal speeds up reactions that turn toxic exhaust gases into harmless ones. Platinum helps convert carbon monoxide and unburned fuel into carbon dioxide and water without being consumed itself, the hallmark of a true catalyst. A modern converter contains only a few grams of platinum-group metals, yet it cleans the exhaust of a vehicle for its entire life.

facts.title: Once the world's master ruler
facts.text: From 1889 to 2019, the kilogram itself was defined by a single cylinder made of 90 percent platinum and 10 percent iridium, kept under three glass bell jars near Paris. Platinum was chosen because it is dense, stable, and almost immune to corrosion, so the artifact would not gain or lose mass over time. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined using the Planck constant, finally retiring this gleaming metal standard.

facts.title: A weapon against cancer
facts.text: Platinum sits at the heart of some of the most important chemotherapy drugs ever made, including cisplatin, discovered to fight tumors by physicist Barnett Rosenberg in the 1960s. These drugs work by binding to the DNA inside cancer cells, kinking the double helix so the cells can no longer divide and multiply. Cisplatin and its relatives are still used today to treat testicular, ovarian, bladder, and other cancers, saving countless lives.

facts.title: Born in cosmic cataclysms
facts.text: Platinum is not made in ordinary stars; the leading explanation is that heavy elements like it are forged when neutron stars collide or in rare violent supernovae. In 2017 astronomers watched two neutron stars merge and detected the chemical signatures of newly created heavy metals in the debris. The platinum in a piece of jewelry was likely created in such a catastrophe billions of years before our Sun was born.

facts.title: Rarer than gold
facts.text: Platinum is far scarcer in the Earth's crust than gold, and roughly three-quarters of the world's supply comes from a single geological formation, the Bushveld Igneous Complex in South Africa. Extracting it is brutally inefficient: producing a single ounce of pure platinum requires mining and processing several tons of ore. This scarcity, combined with deep mining and intensive refining, is a major reason the metal commands such high prices.

facts.title: It drinks hydrogen gas
facts.text: Finely divided platinum, known as platinum black or platinum sponge, can absorb enormous volumes of hydrogen gas relative to its own size and hold it loosely on its surface. This property makes platinum a superb catalyst for reactions involving hydrogen and a key electrode material in hydrogen fuel cells. By splitting hydrogen and oxygen reactions, platinum helps fuel cells generate electricity with water as the only byproduct.

facts.title: Hypoallergenic and eternal
facts.text: Because platinum is so chemically inert, it almost never triggers the skin allergies that nickel-containing alloys can cause, making it a favorite for piercings and fine jewelry. It is also remarkably ductile and strong, so jewelers can hold gemstones securely with thin, durable prongs that resist wear for generations. A gram of platinum can be drawn into a wire over two kilometers long without breaking.
